questions.q_en:
Identify whether the highlighted group of words is a phrase or a clause.

The tourists waited patiently near the entrance of the ancient monument until the gates were opened.
questions.q_hi:
Identify whether the highlighted group of words is a phrase or a clause.

The tourists waited patiently near the entrance of the ancient monument until the gates were opened.
questions.solution_en:
Answer: C) Phrase

Explanation: A phrase is a group of words that does not contain both a subject and a verb together.

The highlighted group: “near the entrance of the ancient monument” does not contain any subject-verb combination.

Therefore, it is a phrase, specifically a prepositional phrase.

questions.q_en: After finishing the first round of the inspection at the construction site, the engineer is noticing several cracks forming near the basement walls.
questions.q_hi: After finishing the first round of the inspection at the construction site, the engineer is noticing several cracks forming near the basement walls
questions.solution_en:
The correct answer is (B) noticed.

📌 Rule: Sequence of Past Events (Finished Action)

When a sentence describes a sequence of events where one action follows another in the past, we use the Simple Past Tense (V2).

The phrase "After finishing" (a gerund phrase acting as a time marker) indicates that the first event (the inspection) was completed. The second event (seeing the cracks) happened immediately following that completion. Both events are part of a past narrative.

💢 Analysis of the Options

  • is noticing (Original): Incorrect. This is Present Continuous. It creates a "Tense Mismatch." You cannot finish a past/narrative inspection and then be "noticing" in the present continuous within the same logical sequence.

  • a) notices: Incorrect. This is Simple Present. It is used for habits or universal truths. It doesn't fit a specific incident at a construction site.

  • b) noticed (Correct): Correct. This is the Simple Past ($V_2$). It matches the narrative flow: Action 1 (Finishing) $\rightarrow$ Action 2 (Noticed).

  • c) had noticed: Incorrect. This is Past Perfect. We use this for the earlier of two past actions. Here, the "noticing" happened after the finishing, not before it.

  • d) was noticed: Incorrect. This is Passive Voice. It would mean the engineer was noticed by someone else, which doesn't make sense here—the engineer is the one doing the looking.

Corrected Sentence

After finishing the first round of inspection at the construction site, the engineer noticed several cracks forming near the basement walls.

questions.q_en:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

Every one of the newly recruited management trainees from the prestigious institute ________ expected to submit ________ detailed research report on market trends by the end of this fiscal year.
questions.q_hi:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

Every one of the newly recruited management trainees from the prestigious institute ________ expected to submit ________ detailed research report on market trends by the end of this fiscal year.
options_en: are / their
is / their
are / his
is / his
options_hi: are / their
is / their
are / his
is / his
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (D)- The blanks should be filled with the singular verb "is" and the singular possessive pronoun "his".

Rule/Concept: Indefinite Pronoun Agreement Indefinite pronouns like "Every one," "Each," "Everyone," and "Nobody" are grammatically singular. They must be followed by a singular verb and a singular possessive pronoun, even if a plural noun (like trainees) comes in between as a qualifier.

Logic Breakdown:

The Main Subject: The subject is "Every one," which is singular. The phrase "of the newly recruited management trainees" is just a qualifier.

Blank 1 (Verb): Since the subject is singular, we must use "is." This eliminates options (A) and (C).

Blank 2 (Pronoun): This is where most students fail. Because the subject is "Every one," we must use the singular pronoun "his" (per standard exam convention) instead of the plural "their". This eliminates option (B).

Agreement: "Every one (Singular) ... is (Singular) ... his (Singular)."

Correct Sentence: Every one of the newly recruited management trainees from the prestigious institute is expected to submit his detailed research report on market trends by the end of this fiscal year.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: sold in this grocery store
are of very poor quality.
options_hi: sold in this grocery store
are of very poor quality.
questions.solution_en:
The error lies in option (A)- It should be "The bread and the butter."

Rule/Concept: Separate Entities vs. A Single Unit When "bread" and "butter" are being discussed as separate commodities being sold or bought (acting differently), they must each have their own article (The). Because there are two distinct items, the sentence then requires a plural verb.

Logic Breakdown:

Often Confused: Students often remember "Bread and butter is my favourite breakfast." This is correct because it's one meal.

The Conflict: In this sentence, the context is a "grocery store." A store sells bread as one item and butter as another separate item.

The Error: Because they are separate products, option (A) must have a second "the" to show plurality.

Corrected Sentence: The bread and the butter sold in this grocery store are of very poor quality.

questions.q_en:
1. You must adept yourself to new situations.

2. He is adept in the art of dancing.
questions.q_hi:
1. You must adept yourself to new situations.

2. He is adept in the art of dancing.
questions.solution_en:
Sentence 1: ❌ You must adept yourself to new situations.
✔ You must adapt yourself to new situations.

Why?

  • Adept = adjective (skilled, proficient)

  • Adapt = verb (to adjust/change)

You need a verb here, so adapt is correct, not adept.

Sentence 2: ✔ He is adept in the art of dancing. ✅

Why?

  • Adept is correctly used as an adjective meaning highly skilled.

  • It is followed by in (sometimes at is also acceptable).

✔ Examples:

  • She is adept in mathematics.

  • He is adept at handling crises.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: The project manager in addition to his assistants
working on the new software development initiative
are attending the international tech conference tomorrow.
No Error
options_hi: The project manager in addition to his assistants
working on the new software development initiative
are attending the international tech conference tomorrow.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (C)

The plural verb "are" must be replaced with the singular verb "is."

Rule/Concept: Parenthetical Phrases (First Subject Rule) When subjects are joined by phrases like in addition to, as well as, along with, together with, or accompanied by, the verb ignores everything that follows these phrases. It must agree strictly with the First Subject.

Logic Breakdown:

Subject 1: "The project manager" (Singular).

Subject 2: "his assistants" (Plural).

The Decision: Because they are joined by "in addition to," the plural "assistants" is treated as extra information. The verb must "jump back" to agree with the singular "manager."

Correct Sentence: The project manager in addition to his assistants working on the new software development initiative is attending the international tech conference tomorrow.

questions.q_en:
Transparency is widely regarded as a cornerstone of democratic governance, yet its practical implementation often proves challenging. Governments may publicly endorse openness, but administrative processes frequently remain [---1---], limiting citizens’ ability to scrutinize decision-making. In some cases, excessive procedural complexity serves to [---2---] accountability rather than enhance it, creating a gap between formal disclosure and meaningful access to information. Such practices can foster public [---3---], as repeated assurances of openness fail to translate into tangible outcomes. Consequently, experts argue that transparency must be treated not as a symbolic gesture but as a [---4---] commitment embedded within institutional culture.

Choose the most appropriate option to fill in the blank [3] :

Such practices can foster public [---3---], as repeated assurances of openness fail to translate into tangible outcomes. Choose the most appropriate option to fill in the blank [3] :
options_en: complacency
cynicism
enthusiasm
reassurance
options_hi: complacency
cynicism
enthusiasm
reassurance
questions.solution_en:
Cynicism refers to distrust or disbelief in sincerity. When promises of openness repeatedly fail, public skepticism naturally turns into cynicism.
WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
• Complacency implies satisfaction, not distrust.
• Enthusiasm suggests optimism, which is contradicted here.
• Reassurance implies confidence, not erosion of trust.

📌 Rule / Concept: Intransitive Verbs and the Passive Voice Trap -

Certain verbs in English are Intransitive, meaning they do not take a direct object. Because they cannot "act upon" something else, they cannot be used in the Passive Voice. Common intransitive verbs frequently tested in SSC/Banking include: Occur, Happen, Emerge, Disappear, Appear, Arrive, Die, Exist.

In the Passive Voice (be + V3), the subject receives the action. However, since these verbs represent things that simply "take place" or "become visible" on their own, using them in the passive form (was occurred, was emerged, will be happened) is a major grammatical error.

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the verb "emerge" is intransitive. The "sense of resentment" is the thing that is doing the emerging; it is not being "emerged" by someone else. Therefore, the helping verb "was" must be removed to keep the sentence in the Active Voice.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1: The accident occurred at midnight. (Not: was occurred)

Example 2: A strange figure appeared in the doorway. (Not: was appeared)

Example 3: What happened to your car? (Not: was happened)

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the verb "emerge" is intransitive. The "sense of resentment" is the thing that is doing the emerging; it is not being "emerged" by someone else. Therefore, the helping verb "was" must be removed to keep the sentence in the Active Voice.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1: The accident occurred at midnight. (Not: was occurred)

Example 2: A strange figure appeared in the doorway. (Not: was appeared)

Example 3: What happened to your car? (Not: was happened)

questions.q_en:
Banks occupy a paradoxical position in modern economies. They are simultaneously engines of growth and custodians of systemic stability. While their primary function is to allocate capital efficiently, their operations are deeply intertwined with public trust, regulatory oversight, and macroeconomic resilience. This dual role becomes particularly visible during periods of financial stress, when decisions taken in the pursuit of profitability can amplify vulnerabilities rather than mitigate them. One persistent banking challenge lies in the tension between credit expansion and risk containment. In growth phases, banks are incentivized to loosen lending standards to capture market share, often relying heavily on optimistic projections and asset valuations. Such practices appear rational in isolation but collectively generate fragility. When economic conditions reverse, non-performing assets rise, capital buffers erode, and balance sheets reveal risks that were previously obscured by growth narratives. Regulatory interventions, though designed to prevent systemic collapse, introduce their own complications. Compliance requirements increase operational costs and can constrain lending, particularly to small and medium enterprises. Moreover, regulation often responds to past crises, leaving banks to navigate new financial instruments and digital risks with frameworks that lag innovation. This regulatory asymmetry fuels debates over whether banks are being overburdened or insufficiently restrained. Compounding these issues is the evolving relationship between banks and technology. Digitalization promises efficiency, financial inclusion, and real-time risk monitoring. Yet it also concentrates operational risks, exposes systems to cyber threats, and alters the traditional bank–customer relationship. As banks increasingly resemble technology-driven service platforms, questions arise about accountability, resilience, and the adequacy of existing safeguards. Ultimately, banking stability depends not merely on stronger regulations or advanced technology, but on institutional judgment. Without disciplined risk culture and transparent governance, banks may continue oscillating between excess and restraint, reinforcing cycles of confidence and crisis rather than breaking them.

"Some of the forensic evidence recovered from the primary crime scenes and the multiple suspects' vehicles _________ been sent to the laboratory for detailed analysis."
questions.q_hi:

"Some of the forensic evidence recovered from the primary crime scenes and the multiple suspects' vehicles _________ been sent to the laboratory for detailed analysis."
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (A)

The singular verb "has" is the only correct choice to match the uncountable subject.

Rule/Concept: "Some of" with Uncountable Nouns The words Some of, Most of, and All of are "transparent." The verb ignores these words and agrees strictly with the noun that follows the preposition "of".

The Subject: The noun after "of" is "evidence."

The Property: "Evidence" is an uncountable noun. In English grammar, uncountable nouns are always singular and never take a plural verb, even if they refer to a large collection of items.

Logic Breakdown

The Distractor: The sentence includes plural nouns like "scenes" and "vehicles" right before the blank. These are placed there to trick your ear into choosing the plural options (B, C, or D).

Correct Sentence: Some of the forensic evidence recovered from the primary crime scenes and the multiple suspects' vehicles has been sent to the laboratory...

questions.solution_en:
The correct answer is (c) No improvement required.

📌 Rule: Parallelism after "To" (Infinitives)

When you use the word "to" to join two or more verbs (to express purpose or intent), it creates an infinitive structure. Both verbs must be in the base form (V1).

The structure is: To + [Base Verb 1] + and + [Base Verb 2].

💢 Analysis of the Options

  • Original Sentence (c): "...to improve (V1) and enhance (V1)..."

    • This is perfectly correct. The "to" applies to both "improve" and "enhance." Think of it as: to improve and (to) enhance.

  • a) have promised to improve and enhanced:

    • Incorrect. This violates the rule of parallelism. You cannot have a V1(improve) and a V2/V3 (enhanced) connected by "and" under the same "to."

  • b) has promised to improve and enhance:

    • Incorrect. The subject is "The university authorities" (plural). Therefore, you must use the plural helping verb "have," not the singular "has."

  • d) have promise to improve and enhance:

    • Incorrect. After the helping verb "have," we must use the Past Participle (V3). It should be "have promised," not "have promise."

questions.q_hi:
The following sentence contains a blank space, followed by four alternative options. You are required to choose the most appropriate option (A, B, C, or D) that grammatically completes the sentence in accordance with the rules of English grammar.

"No supervisor and no manager from the local branch office _________ authorized to access the confidential database without obtaining prior clearance from the director."
options_en: Both A or B
options_hi: Both A or B
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (A)

The singular verb "was" is the only grammatically correct choice for this construction.

Rule/Concept: "No" with Singular Nouns joined by "And" When two singular nouns are joined by "and" and are both preceded by the word "No," the subject is considered singular. It implies "not even one person" from either category, hence the verb must be Singular.

Logic Breakdown:

The Subject: "No supervisor and no manager." Even though they are joined by "and," the presence of "No" makes the count zero. In grammar, this specific negative construction requires a singular verb.

The Distractor: The phrase "from the local branch office" adds length to move the verb away from the subject.

Correct Sentence: No supervisor and no manager from the local branch office was authorized to access the confidential database without obtaining prior clearance from the director.
